lead: Probability turns uncertainty into numbers between 0 and 1. A random experiment has outcomes; the set of all outcomes is the sample space Ω. An event is a subset of Ω. Three axioms fix how probability behaves on these sets. From them we derive useful rules: the probability of the empty set is 0, the complement rule, and the addition rule for A∪B. Engineers use these rules when they estimate failure rates, queue overload, or the chance that a UPI payment fails. The same language prepares you for conditional probability and random variables later.
prereq: You need: basic set notation (∈, ⊆, ∪, ∩, complement) and fractions; Unit 1 descriptive statistics is context only.

blocks.text: A random experiment is a process with a known set of possible results and an uncertain result on any one run. One result is an outcome, written ω. The sample space Ω is the set of all outcomes. An event A is a subset of Ω: A⊆Ω. The sure event is Ω itself; the impossible event is ∅. Some syllabi call Ω the universal set and events subsets of it.

Events combine like sets. A∪B is the event that A or B or both occur. A∩B is the event that both occur. Aᶜ is the complement: A does not occur. A−B is A∩Bᶜ: A occurs and B does not. De Morgan's laws hold: (A∪B)ᶜ=Aᶜ∩Bᶜ and (A∩B)ᶜ=Aᶜ∪Bᶜ.

Two events are mutually exclusive if A∩B=∅; they cannot occur together. They are exhaustive if A∪B=Ω; together they cover every outcome. For a die, A={2,4,6} and B={3,6} are not mutually exclusive because 6 is in both. C={1,3,5} and A are mutually exclusive and exhaustive for Ω={1,2,3,4,5,6}.
The three axioms are the definition. For every event A in Ω:

items: If A₁,A₂,... are pairwise disjoint (Aᵢ∩Aⱼ=∅ for i≠j), then P(A₁∪A₂∪...)=ΣP(Aᵢ).

blocks.text: Derive two facts. Ω and ∅ are disjoint and Ω∪∅=Ω, so 1=P(Ω)=P(Ω)+P(∅), giving P(∅)=0. A and Aᶜ are disjoint and A∪Aᶜ=Ω, so 1=P(A)+P(Aᶜ), giving P(Aᶜ)=1−P(A).

blocks.where: P(A) is the probability of event A; P(B) is the probability of event B; P(A∩B) is the probability that both A and B occur. If A∩B=∅, then P(A∩B)=0 and P(A∪B)=P(A)+P(B).

blocks.text: Write A∪B as A∪(B∩Aᶜ); these are disjoint. Also B=(B∩A)∪(B∩Aᶜ), disjoint. So P(A∪B)=P(A)+P(B∩Aᶜ)=P(A)+P(B)−P(A∩B). If A⊆B, then B=A∪(B∩Aᶜ) with disjoint parts, so P(B)=P(A)+P(B∩Aᶜ)≥P(A). This is monotonicity.

For equally likely outcomes, P(A)=|A|/|Ω|, where |A| is the number of outcomes in A. For repeated trials, relative frequency n(A)/n often settles near P(A) as n grows. These motivate the axioms but do not replace them. Conditional probability later restricts Ω to an event B: see Conditional probability and independent events.

Three rules solve most first-step problems. Write Ω and list the outcomes. Write each event as a set. If outcomes are equally likely, count outcomes: P(A)=|A|/|Ω|. For a fair die, |Ω|=6, so each single outcome has probability 1/6. Relative frequency is not a proof; the axioms are the definition.

blocks.text: The addition rule is the one examiners test most: subtract P(A∩B) once because A and B both contain it. If A and B are mutually exclusive, P(A∩B)=0 and the subtraction disappears.

examples.question: A fair six-sided die is rolled once. The sample space is Ω={1,2,3,4,5,6}. Let A={2,4,6} and B={3,6}. Find P(A), P(B), P(A∩B), P(A∪B), and P(Aᶜ).
steps: Each outcome is equally likely, so P({k})=1/6 for k=1,2,3,4,5,6.
By the complement rule, P(Aᶜ)=1−P(A)=1−1/2=1/2. Check: Aᶜ={1,3,5}, which has 3 outcomes, and 3/6=1/2.

traps: Adding P(A)+P(B) counts A∩B twice. Subtract P(A∩B) once.
Events are sets of outcomes, not single outcomes. P(A) is not the probability of one outcome in A.
P(∅)=0 is derived from the axioms, not a fourth axiom in the standard list.
Mutually exclusive (A∩B=∅) is not the same as independent. Independence comes in Conditional probability and independent events.
The complement is taken inside Ω. P(Aᶜ)=1−P(A) only when Aᶜ means 'not A within Ω'.

quiz.q: Define sample space and event. Give one example for a single die.
quiz.a: The sample space Ω is the set of all outcomes. An event A is a subset of Ω. For a die, Ω={1,2,3,4,5,6}; A={2,4,6} is the event 'even result'.

quiz.q: State the three axioms of probability.
quiz.a: P(Ω)=1; P(A)≥0 for every event A; for pairwise disjoint A₁,A₂,..., P(A₁∪A₂∪...)=ΣP(Aᵢ).

quiz.q: Why is P(∅)=0? Derive it from the axioms.
quiz.a: Ω and ∅ are disjoint and Ω∪∅=Ω. Axiom 1 and the disjoint sum give 1=P(Ω)=P(Ω)+P(∅). Hence P(∅)=0.

quiz.q: A fair die is rolled. Let A={1,3,5} and B={3,4}. Find P(A∪B) and P(Aᶜ).
Two fair coins are tossed. Ω={HH,HT,TH,TT}. Let A={at least one head}, B={exactly one head}. Find P(A), P(B), P(A∩B), P(A∪B).
Prove monotonicity: if A⊆B then P(A)≤P(B).
quiz.a: Write B=A∪(B∩Aᶜ). The two parts are disjoint. So P(B)=P(A)+P(B∩Aᶜ). Since P(B∩Aᶜ)≥0, P(B)≥P(A).

quiz.q: P(A)=0.6 and P(B)=0.5. A student writes P(A∪B)=1.1. Explain the error and give the correct formula with P(A∩B).
quiz.a: The student added P(A)+P(B) and forgot to subtract the overlap. The correct rule is P(A∪B)=P(A)+P(B)−P(A∩B)=1.1−P(A∩B). Since P(A∪B)≤1, P(A∩B)≥0.1.

beyond: Not for the exam. Measure theory replaces the collection of all subsets with a sigma-algebra, so probability lives on a space (Ω, F, P). This matters when Ω is uncountable, such as all real voltages in a circuit. The axioms then define a probability measure, and events are the sets in F. Search for 'Kolmogorov axioms', 'sigma-algebra', and 'probability space'. The same ideas support stochastic processes and uncertainty quantification in machine learning.
